\mathfrak{m} = R_1 \times \cdots \times \mathfrak{m}_j \times \cdots \times R_k,
\]
where \(\mathfrak{m}_j\) is a maximal ideal of exactly one factor \(R_j\); this holds because the projection \(R \to R_j\) is surjective and the remaining factors contribute the whole ring to keep the quotient a field. Since each \(R_j\) contributes only finitely many maximal ideals, the total number of maximal ideals of \(R\) is the finite sum of these counts, and \(R\) is semi-local.

blocks.label: Examples
items: Every local ring, in particular every field, is semi-local, having exactly one maximal ideal.
The ring \(\mathbb{Z}/720\mathbb{Z}\) is semi-local: since \(720 = 2^4 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5\), its maximal ideals correspond to the primes \(2, 3, 5\), so there are exactly three.
The localization of \(\mathbb{Z}\) at the multiplicatively closed set of integers coprime to \(6\) is semi-local with the two maximal ideals generated by \(2\) and by \(3\).
The ring \(\mathbb{Z}\) itself is not semi-local: it has infinitely many maximal ideals \((p)\), one for each prime \(p\).
A finite product of fields \(k_1 \times \cdots \times k_n\) is semi-local with exactly \(n\) maximal ideals.

concepts.title: Jacobson radical
concepts.inline: The Jacobson radical of a ring is the intersection of all its maximal ideals.

concepts.title: Radical Ideal
concepts.inline: The radical of an ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) in a commutative ring \(R\) is the set \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) of elements some power of which lies in \(\mathfrak{a}\); an ideal equal to its own radical is called a radical ideal.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: In the ring \(\mathbb{Z}\), knowing that \(x^2\) is divisible by \(12\) does not tell you that \(x\) is divisible by \(12\): take \(x=6\), where \(x^2=36\) is a multiple of \(12\) but \(x\) is not. Yet if \(x^2\) is divisible by a squarefree number like \(30\), then \(x\) itself must be. Something distinguishes ideals that detect roots from those that do not, and the offending elements are exactly those whose powers slip into the ideal even though they themselves stay out. To measure this failure we collect every element with a power inside \(\mathfrak{a}\), forming a larger set that repairs the defect. The question of when an ideal already contains all such elements — when it cannot be enlarged this way — leads inevitably to the notion of a radical ideal.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(\mathfrak{a}\) an ideal of \(R\). The radical of \(\mathfrak{a}\) is
\[\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}} = \{\, x \in R : x^n \in \mathfrak{a} \text{ for some integer } n \geq 1 \,\}.\]
The ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) is called a radical ideal if \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}} = \mathfrak{a}\).
blocks.proof:
We verify that \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) is an ideal of \(R\). Since \(0 = 0^1 \in \mathfrak{a}\), we have \(0 \in \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\). Suppose \(x, y \in \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\), say \(x^m \in \mathfrak{a}\) and \(y^n \in \mathfrak{a}\). Expanding by the binomial theorem,
\[(x+y)^{m+n-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{m+n-1} \binom{m+n-1}{k} x^k y^{m+n-1-k}.\]
In each term either \(k \geq m\) or \(m+n-1-k \geq n\), for otherwise \(k \leq m-1\) and \(m+n-1-k \leq n-1\) would give \(m+n-1 = k + (m+n-1-k) \leq (m-1)+(n-1) = m+n-2\), a contradiction. Hence every term contains either a factor \(x^m\) or a factor \(y^n\), so each term lies in \(\mathfrak{a}\), whence \((x+y)^{m+n-1} \in \mathfrak{a}\) and \(x+y \in \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\). Finally, if \(x \in \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) with \(x^m \in \mathfrak{a}\) and \(r \in R\), then \((rx)^m = r^m x^m \in \mathfrak{a}\) since \(\mathfrak{a}\) is an ideal, so \(rx \in \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\). Thus \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) is an ideal, and it contains \(\mathfrak{a}\) because \(x \in \mathfrak{a}\) gives \(x^1 \in \mathfrak{a}\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: The radical \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) is the intersection of all prime ideals of \(R\) containing \(\mathfrak{a}\).
An ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) is radical if and only if the quotient ring \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) is reduced, that is, has no nonzero nilpotent elements.

Under the correspondence between ideals of \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) and ideals of \(R\) containing \(\mathfrak{a}\), the radical \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) is the preimage of the nilradical of \(R/\mathfrak{a}\).
blocks.proof:
Write \(\pi\colon R \to R/\mathfrak{a}\) for the quotient map. An element \(x \in R\) satisfies \(x^n \in \mathfrak{a}\) for some \(n\) if and only if \(\pi(x)^n = 0\) in \(R/\mathfrak{a}\), i.e. \(\pi(x)\) is nilpotent. Hence \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}} = \pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{N})\) where \(\mathfrak{N}\) is the nilradical of \(R/\mathfrak{a}\); this establishes the third characterization. Consequently \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}} = \mathfrak{a}\) holds exactly when \(\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{N}) = \mathfrak{a} = \pi^{-1}(0)\), i.e. when \(\mathfrak{N} = 0\), which means \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) is reduced; this gives the second characterization.

For the first, recall that the nilradical of any commutative ring equals the intersection of all its prime ideals. Applying this to \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) and pulling back along \(\pi\), and using that the primes of \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) correspond bijectively to the primes of \(R\) containing \(\mathfrak{a}\), we obtain
\[\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}} = \pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{N}) = \pi^{-1}\Big(\bigcap_{\bar{\mathfrak{p}}} \bar{\mathfrak{p}}\Big) = \bigcap_{\mathfrak{p} \supseteq \mathfrak{a}} \mathfrak{p},\]
the intersection ranging over prime ideals \(\mathfrak{p}\) of \(R\) containing \(\mathfrak{a}\). To prove the underlying fact that the nilradical is the intersection of all primes: if \(x\) is nilpotent then \(x^n = 0\) lies in every prime \(\mathfrak{p}\), and primeness forces \(x \in \mathfrak{p}\); conversely if \(x\) is not nilpotent, consider the multiplicatively closed set \(S = \{1, x, x^2, \dots\}\), which does not contain \(0\). By Zorn's lemma choose an ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) maximal among those disjoint from \(S\); such \(\mathfrak{p}\) is prime, for if \(a,b \notin \mathfrak{p}\) then \(\mathfrak{p}+(a)\) and \(\mathfrak{p}+(b)\) both meet \(S\), giving powers \(x^i, x^j \in \mathfrak{p}+(a), \mathfrak{p}+(b)\), and multiplying shows \(\mathfrak{p}+(ab)\) meets \(S\), so \(ab \notin \mathfrak{p}\). This prime avoids \(x\), so \(x\) lies outside the intersection of all primes.

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: Every prime ideal is a radical ideal, and the radical operation satisfies \(\sqrt{\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}} = \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\), so \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) is always a radical ideal — indeed the smallest radical ideal containing \(\mathfrak{a}\).
blocks.proof:
If \(\mathfrak{p}\) is prime and \(x^n \in \mathfrak{p}\), then by primeness, applied inductively to \(x \cdot x^{n-1} \in \mathfrak{p}\), we conclude \(x \in \mathfrak{p}\); thus \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{p}} \subseteq \mathfrak{p}\), and since always \(\mathfrak{p} \subseteq \sqrt{\mathfrak{p}}\), we get \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{p}} = \mathfrak{p}\).

Now we show \(\sqrt{\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}} = \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\). The inclusion \(\supseteq\) holds because \(\mathfrak{b} \subseteq \sqrt{\mathfrak{b}}\) for any ideal \(\mathfrak{b}\). For \(\subseteq\), suppose \(x \in \sqrt{\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}}\), so \(x^n \in \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) for some \(n \geq 1\); then \((x^n)^m \in \mathfrak{a}\) for some \(m \geq 1\), whence \(x^{nm} \in \mathfrak{a}\) and \(x \in \sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\). Thus \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) equals its own radical and is a radical ideal. Finally, if \(\mathfrak{b}\) is any radical ideal with \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq \mathfrak{b}\), then taking radicals gives \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}} \subseteq \sqrt{\mathfrak{b}} = \mathfrak{b}\), so \(\sqrt{\mathfrak{a}}\) is the smallest radical ideal containing \(\mathfrak{a}\).

blocks.label: Examples
items: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), the radical of \((n)\) is \((m)\) where \(m\) is the product of the distinct primes dividing \(n\); for instance \(\sqrt{(12)} = (6)\) and \(\sqrt{(72)} = (6)\). Thus \((n)\) is radical precisely when \(n\) is squarefree.
The radical of the zero ideal is the nilradical: \(\sqrt{(0)} = \mathfrak{N}(R)\). Hence \((0)\) is a radical ideal exactly when \(R\) is reduced.
Every maximal ideal is radical, since maximal ideals are prime and prime ideals are radical.

In the polynomial ring \(k[x,y]\), the ideal \((x^2, y)\) is not radical: its radical is the maximal ideal \((x,y)\), because \(x^2 \in (x^2,y)\) shows \(x \in \sqrt{(x^2,y)}\) while \(x \notin (x^2,y)\).

concepts.inline: A ring map is a ring homomorphism, a function between rings preserving addition, multiplication, and the identity.

concepts.title: vector space
concepts.inline: A vector space over a field \(F\) is an abelian group equipped with a scalar multiplication by elements of \(F\) satisfying distributivity and associativity axioms.

concepts.title: group endomorphism
concepts.inline: A group endomorphism of \(M\) is a group homomorphism from \(M\) to itself.

concepts.title: endomorphism ring
concepts.inline: The endomorphism ring of an abelian group \(M\) is the ring \(\operatorname{End}(M)\) of group homomorphisms \(M \to M\) under pointwise addition and composition.

concepts.title: R-submodules
concepts.inline: An \(R\)-submodule of an \(R\)-module \(M\) is a subgroup of \(M\) closed under the scalar action of \(R\).

concepts.title: free module
concepts.inline: A free module of rank \(n\) over a ring \(R\) is an \(R\)-module isomorphic to \(R^n\) with componentwise operations.

concepts.title: Faithful Module
concepts.inline: An \(R\)-module \(M\) is faithful if no nonzero ring element acts as zero on all of \(M\); equivalently, its annihilator \(\mathrm{Ann}_R(M)\) is the zero ideal.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: A module over \(R\) is really a way of letting the ring act on an abelian group, one element of \(R\) at a time. But nothing forces distinct ring elements to act differently: in \(\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}\) viewed as a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-module, the integer \(6\) sends every element to \(0\), so this module simply cannot see the difference between \(6\) and \(0\). In effect the module perceives a smaller ring than the one it is defined over, and part of \(R\) becomes invisible. It is natural to isolate those modules that hide nothing — where the only element acting as zero really is zero — so that the action mirrors the ring exactly. Once we ask which elements act trivially, we are already looking at the annihilator, and the condition that it vanish writes itself down.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(M\) an \(R\)-module. The annihilator of \(M\) is
\[ \mathrm{Ann}_R(M) = \{\, r \in R : rm = 0 \text{ for all } m \in M \,\}, \]
which is an ideal of \(R\). The module \(M\) is called faithful if \(\mathrm{Ann}_R(M) = 0\), that is, if the only \(r \in R\) with \(rM = 0\) is \(r = 0\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: The structure map \(\lambda \colon R \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)\) sending \(r\) to the additive endomorphism \(m \mapsto rm\) is injective.
For every nonzero \(r \in R\) there exists some \(m \in M\) with \(rm \neq 0\).
blocks.proof: The scalar multiplication of \(M\) determines a ring homomorphism \(\lambda \colon R \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)\) into the endomorphism ring of the underlying abelian group, given by \(\lambda(r)(m) = rm\); the module axioms are precisely the statement that \(\lambda\) respects addition and multiplication and sends \(1\) to the identity. Now \(r \in \ker(\lambda)\) means \(\lambda(r) = 0\), i.e. \(rm = 0\) for all \(m \in M\), which is exactly the condition \(r \in \mathrm{Ann}_R(M)\). Hence \(\ker(\lambda) = \mathrm{Ann}_R(M)\), and \(\lambda\) is injective if and only if \(\mathrm{Ann}_R(M) = 0\), which is the definition of faithfulness. The second characterization is merely the contrapositive of membership in the annihilator: \(\mathrm{Ann}_R(M) = 0\) says that no nonzero \(r\) kills all of \(M\), equivalently every nonzero \(r\) fails to annihilate some \(m\).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: For any \(R\)-module \(M\), the module \(M\) carries a natural structure of module over the quotient ring \(R/\mathrm{Ann}_R(M)\), and as such it is faithful. Thus every module is faithful over the quotient of its coefficient ring by its annihilator.
blocks.proof: Write \(\mathfrak{a} = \mathrm{Ann}_R(M)\), an ideal of \(R\). Define an action of \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) on \(M\) by \((r + \mathfrak{a})\cdot m = rm\). This is well defined: if \(r + \mathfrak{a} = r' + \mathfrak{a}\), then \(r - r' \in \mathfrak{a}\), so \((r-r')m = 0\) for every \(m \in M\), whence \(rm = r'm\). The module axioms for this action follow immediately from those of the original \(R\)-action, since they are verified representative-wise; for instance associativity reads \((r+\mathfrak a)(r'+\mathfrak a)\cdot m = (rr')m = r(r'm) = (r+\mathfrak a)\cdot\big((r'+\mathfrak a)\cdot m\big)\). It remains to compute the annihilator of \(M\) as an \(R/\mathfrak{a}\)-module. An element \(r + \mathfrak{a}\) annihilates \(M\) if and only if \(rm = 0\) for all \(m \in M\), i.e. if and only if \(r \in \mathfrak{a}\), i.e. if and only if \(r + \mathfrak{a} = 0\) in \(R/\mathfrak{a}\). Therefore \(\mathrm{Ann}_{R/\mathfrak{a}}(M) = 0\), so \(M\) is a faithful \(R/\mathfrak{a}\)-module.

blocks.label: Examples
items: The ring \(R\) regarded as a module over itself is faithful, since \(r\cdot 1 = r\) forces \(\mathrm{Ann}_R(R) = 0\).
Every free module \(R^{(I)}\) with \(I \neq \varnothing\) is faithful, as any \(r\) annihilating it must annihilate a basis element, hence equal \(0\).
The \(\mathbb{Z}\)-module \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) with \(n > 1\) is not faithful: its annihilator is \(n\mathbb{Z} \neq 0\).
A cyclic module \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) has annihilator \(\mathfrak{a}\), so it is faithful over \(R\) if and only if \(\mathfrak{a} = 0\).
Any vector space over a field \(k\), if nonzero, is faithful, because the only ideals of \(k\) are \(0\) and \(k\), and \(1\) does not annihilate a nonzero vector.

concepts.title: Annihilator
concepts.inline: The annihilator of an \(R\)-module \(M\) is the set of ring elements \(r\) with \(rM = 0\); it is a two-sided ideal of \(R\) measuring how far the module is from being faithful.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: When \(R\) acts on an abelian group \(M\), some scalars may do nothing at all: multiplication by \(2\) kills every element of \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\), and multiplication by \(6\) kills every element of \(\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}\). This is not an accident of a single element but a phenomenon shared by the whole module, and it suggests the ring \(R\) is really acting through a smaller quotient. If we want to know which scalars are genuinely visible to \(M\), and which are wasted, we need to collect all the scalars that annihilate everything at once. Doing so isolates the exact obstruction to \(R\) faithfully controlling \(M\), and it turns out that this collection is itself an ideal — the object we now define.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) be a ring and \(M\) a left \(R\)-module. The annihilator of \(M\) is
\[\operatorname{Ann}_R(M) = \{\, r \in R : rm = 0 \text{ for all } m \in M \,\}.\]
More generally, for a subset \(S \subseteq M\) one writes \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(S) = \{\, r \in R : rs = 0 \text{ for all } s \in S \,\}\), and for a single element \(m\) one writes \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(m) = \{\, r \in R : rm = 0 \,\}\).
blocks.proof: We verify that \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\) is a two-sided ideal of \(R\). It is nonempty since \(0 \cdot m = 0\) for all \(m\), so \(0 \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\). If \(r, s \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\), then for every \(m \in M\) we have \((r-s)m = rm - sm = 0 - 0 = 0\), hence \(r - s \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\), so it is an additive subgroup. For left absorption, let \(a \in R\) and \(r \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\); then \((ar)m = a(rm) = a \cdot 0 = 0\) for all \(m\), so \(ar \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\). For right absorption, \((ra)m = r(am) = 0\) because \(am \in M\) and \(r\) kills every element of \(M\); thus \(ra \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\). Therefore \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\) is a two-sided ideal.

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\) is the kernel of the ring homomorphism \(R \to \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)\) sending each \(r\) to the multiplication map \(m \mapsto rm\).
\(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M) = \bigcap_{m \in M} \operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\), the intersection of the annihilators of all elements of \(M\).
\(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\) is the largest ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) of \(R\) such that \(M\) is a module over the quotient \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) via the induced action.
blocks.proof: For the first characterization, the module structure of \(M\) is precisely a ring homomorphism \(\varphi : R \to \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M)\), \(\varphi(r)(m) = rm\). Now \(r \in \ker(\varphi)\) if and only if \(\varphi(r)\) is the zero endomorphism, i.e. \(rm = 0\) for all \(m \in M\), which is exactly the condition \(r \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\). For the second characterization, \(r\) kills every \(m \in M\) if and only if \(r \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\) for each individual \(m\), which is the definition of membership in \(\bigcap_{m \in M} \operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\). For the third characterization, first note that if \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\) then the action \((r + \mathfrak{a}) \cdot m := rm\) is well defined, since \(r + \mathfrak{a} = r' + \mathfrak{a}\) gives \(r - r' \in \mathfrak{a} \subseteq \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\), whence \((r - r')m = 0\) and \(rm = r'm\); this makes \(M\) an \(R/\mathfrak{a}\)-module. Conversely, if the action of \(R\) factors through \(R/\mathfrak{a}\), then every element of \(\mathfrak{a}\) acts as zero on \(M\), forcing \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\). Hence \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\) is the largest such ideal, and \(M\) is naturally a faithful \(R/\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\)-module.

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: If \(M\) is a cyclic module, say \(M = Rm\) for some \(m \in M\), then \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M) = \operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\), and there is an isomorphism of \(R\)-modules \(M \cong R/\operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\). Moreover \(M\) is faithful if and only if \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M) = 0\).
blocks.proof: Suppose \(M = Rm\). Since \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M) \subseteq \operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\) trivially, it suffices to prove the reverse inclusion. Let \(r \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\), so \(rm = 0\). Any element of \(M\) has the form \(am\) for some \(a \in R\); assuming \(R\) is commutative we compute \(r(am) = a(rm) = a \cdot 0 = 0\), so \(r\) annihilates all of \(M\) and thus \(r \in \operatorname{Ann}_R(M)\). Hence \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M) = \operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\). Now define \(\psi : R \to M\) by \(\psi(a) = am\). This is a surjective \(R\)-module homomorphism because \(M = Rm\), and its kernel is exactly \(\{a \in R : am = 0\} = \operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\). The first isomorphism theorem gives \(M \cong R/\operatorname{Ann}_R(m)\). Finally, faithfulness of \(M\) means by definition that no nonzero scalar acts as zero on all of \(M\), i.e. \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M) = 0\).

blocks.label: Examples
items: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), the module \(M = \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) has \(\operatorname{Ann}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M) = n\mathbb{Z}\), recovering \(n\) as the generator of the annihilator ideal.

For \(M = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\) over \(\mathbb{Z}\), we get \(\operatorname{Ann}(M) = 2\mathbb{Z} \cap 3\mathbb{Z} = 6\mathbb{Z}\), the least common multiple of the orders.
Any ring \(R\), viewed as a module over itself, is faithful: \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(R) = 0\), since \(r \cdot 1 = r = 0\) forces \(r = 0\).
For a vector space \(V\) over a field \(k\), \(\operatorname{Ann}_k(V) = 0\) whenever \(V \neq 0\), because a field has no nonzero elements acting as zero.
The annihilator of the zero module is all of \(R\): \(\operatorname{Ann}_R(0) = R\).

concepts.title: cyclic module
concepts.inline: A cyclic module is a module generated by a single element, hence isomorphic to \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) for some ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\).
A two-sided ideal of a ring \(R\) is an additive subgroup closed under multiplication by ring elements on both sides.
A left \(R\)-module is an abelian group with a left action of a ring \(R\) compatible with its structure.

concepts.title: zero module
concepts.inline: The zero module is the module consisting of a single element \(0\).

concepts.title: Algebra over a Ring
concepts.inline: An algebra over a commutative ring \(R\) is a ring \(A\) equipped with a ring homomorphism \(R \to A\) landing in the center of \(A\), so that \(A\) is simultaneously a ring and an \(R\)-module whose two multiplications are compatible.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: You already know two ways to enrich a set with structure: you can make it a ring, giving it its own multiplication, or you can make it a module over a base ring \(R\), letting scalars from \(R\) act. But countless objects carry both at once. The polynomial ring \(R[x]\) multiplies polynomials together and also scales them by elements of \(R\); the complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\) multiply and also scale by reals; matrices over a field both multiply and absorb field scalars. In each case the scalar action and the internal multiplication are not independent — scaling a product should be the same as scaling either factor. Without a single notion that packages these two structures together and demands they cooperate, we would keep reproving the same compatibility by hand; the natural move is to fix the base ring \(R\) once and define an object that is a ring and an \(R\)-module at the same time.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. An \(R\)-algebra is a ring \(A\) together with a ring homomorphism \(\varphi\colon R \to A\), called the structure map, whose image lies in the center of \(A\), that is \(\varphi(r)a = a\varphi(r)\) for all \(r \in R\) and \(a \in A\). A homomorphism of \(R\)-algebras \(f\colon A \to B\) is a ring homomorphism satisfying \(f \circ \varphi_A = \varphi_B\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: An \(R\)-algebra is an \(R\)-module \(A\) equipped with an \(R\)-bilinear multiplication \(A \times A \to A\) that is associative and has a multiplicative identity, so that the ring multiplication and the scalar multiplication are linked by \(r(ab) = (ra)b = a(rb)\) for all \(r \in R\) and \(a,b \in A\).
When \(A\) is commutative, an \(R\)-algebra structure on \(A\) is exactly the same data as a ring homomorphism \(R \to A\), since the centrality condition is automatic.
blocks.proof:
Suppose first that \(A\) is an \(R\)-algebra in the sense of the primary definition, with structure map \(\varphi\colon R \to A\) whose image is central. Define a scalar multiplication by \(r \cdot a := \varphi(r)a\). Since \(\varphi\) is a ring homomorphism and \(A\) is an abelian group under addition, this makes \(A\) an \(R\)-module: \((r+s)\cdot a = \varphi(r+s)a = (\varphi(r)+\varphi(s))a = r\cdot a + s\cdot a\), \(r\cdot(a+b) = \varphi(r)(a+b) = r\cdot a + r\cdot b\), \((rs)\cdot a = \varphi(rs)a = \varphi(r)\varphi(s)a = r\cdot(s\cdot a)\), and \(1_R \cdot a = \varphi(1_R)a = 1_A a = a\). The ring multiplication of \(A\) is by definition associative with unit, and it is \(R\)-bilinear: using centrality, \[ r\cdot(ab) = \varphi(r)(ab) = (\varphi(r)a)b = (r\cdot a)b, \] and also \(r\cdot(ab) = \varphi(r)(ab) = a(\varphi(r)b) = a(r\cdot b)\), where the middle step uses \(\varphi(r)(ab) = (a\varphi(r))b = a(\varphi(r)b)\) by centrality of \(\varphi(r)\). This yields precisely the second description.

Conversely, suppose \(A\) is an \(R\)-module with an associative, unital, \(R\)-bilinear multiplication. Define \(\varphi\colon R \to A\) by \(\varphi(r) = r\cdot 1_A\). Then \(\varphi(r+s) = (r+s)\cdot 1_A = r\cdot 1_A + s\cdot 1_A = \varphi(r)+\varphi(s)\), and \(\varphi(1_R) = 1_R \cdot 1_A = 1_A\). Multiplicativity follows from bilinearity: \[ \varphi(rs) = (rs)\cdot 1_A = r\cdot(s\cdot 1_A) = r\cdot(1_A (s\cdot 1_A)) = (r\cdot 1_A)(s\cdot 1_A) = \varphi(r)\varphi(s), \] using \(r\cdot(xy) = (r\cdot x)y\) with \(x = 1_A\), \(y = s\cdot 1_A\). Finally \(\varphi(r)\) is central because for any \(a \in A\), \[ \varphi(r)a = (r\cdot 1_A)a = r\cdot(1_A a) = r\cdot a = r\cdot(a 1_A) = a(r\cdot 1_A) = a\varphi(r), \] again by bilinearity. Thus the two definitions carry exactly the same information. The commutative case is immediate: if \(A\) is commutative, centrality of \(\varphi(R)\) holds trivially, so an \(R\)-algebra structure is nothing more than a ring homomorphism \(R \to A\).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: For every commutative ring \(R\) there is a unique \(R\)-algebra homomorphism from \(R\) to any \(R\)-algebra \(A\); that is, \(R\) itself, with structure map the identity, is the initial object in the category of \(R\)-algebras.
blocks.proof: Let \(A\) be an \(R\)-algebra with structure map \(\varphi\colon R \to A\), and regard \(R\) as an \(R\)-algebra via the identity map \(\mathrm{id}_R\colon R \to R\). An \(R\)-algebra homomorphism \(f\colon R \to A\) must by definition satisfy \(f \circ \mathrm{id}_R = \varphi\), which forces \(f = \varphi\). Hence there is at most one such homomorphism. Conversely, \(\varphi\) itself is a ring homomorphism, and it trivially satisfies the compatibility condition \(\varphi \circ \mathrm{id}_R = \varphi\), so it is an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism. Therefore \(\varphi\) is the unique \(R\)-algebra map \(R \to A\), proving that \(R\) is initial.

blocks.label: Examples
items: Every ring \(A\) is canonically a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra, since there is a unique ring homomorphism \(\mathbb{Z} \to A\) sending \(1\) to \(1_A\); thus \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebras are just rings.
The polynomial ring \(R[x_1,\dots,x_n]\) is an \(R\)-algebra via the inclusion of constants \(R \hookrightarrow R[x_1,\dots,x_n]\).
If \(K\) is a field, then \(\mathbb{C}\) is an \(\mathbb{R}\)-algebra and, more generally, any field extension \(L/K\) makes \(L\) a \(K\)-algebra.

The \(n \times n\) matrix ring \(M_n(R)\) is an \(R\)-algebra with structure map \(r \mapsto r I_n\); here \(A\) is noncommutative for \(n \geq 2\), illustrating why the centrality condition is needed.
Any quotient \(A/\mathfrak{a}\) of an \(R\)-algebra \(A\) by a two-sided ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) is again an \(R\)-algebra, with structure map the composite \(R \to A \to A/\mathfrak{a}\).

concepts.title: matrix ring
concepts.inline: The matrix ring \(M_n(R)\) is the ring of \(n \times n\) matrices with entries in a ring \(R\) under matrix addition and multiplication.

concepts.title: Algebra Homomorphism
concepts.inline: An algebra homomorphism between two \(R\)-algebras is a ring homomorphism that respects the underlying \(R\)-module structure, i.e. that commutes with the two structure maps from \(R\).

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Once we agree to study an \(R\)-algebra \(A\) — a ring that also carries an action of a base ring \(R\) — we immediately want to compare two of them. A bare ring homomorphism between \(A\) and \(B\) remembers the multiplication but may completely forget that both sit over the same \(R\): it could send the scalar copy of \(R\) inside \(A\) somewhere incompatible with the scalar copy inside \(B\). For instance, a map of \(\mathbb{C}\)-algebras that secretly conjugates \(\mathbb{C}\) is a ring map but betrays the \(\mathbb{C}\)-structure we care about. We therefore need a notion of morphism that is simultaneously a ring map and a map of \(R\)-modules, so that scalars are transported faithfully. Demanding compatibility with the structure maps is the only honest way to keep track of the base ring, and the definition below is exactly that demand.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and let \(A, B\) be \(R\)-algebras with structure homomorphisms \(\alpha \colon R \to A\) and \(\beta \colon R \to B\). An \(R\)-algebra homomorphism is a ring homomorphism \(\varphi \colon A \to B\) such that \(\varphi \circ \alpha = \beta\); that is, the diagram of structure maps commutes:
(i) \(\varphi(xy) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y)\) for all \(x,y \in A\),
(ii) \(\varphi(x+y) = \varphi(x) + \varphi(y)\) for all \(x,y \in A\),
(iii) \(\varphi(1_A) = 1_B\),
(iv) \(\varphi(\alpha(r)) = \beta(r)\) for all \(r \in R\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: A map \(\varphi \colon A \to B\) is an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism if and only if it is simultaneously a ring homomorphism and a homomorphism of \(R\)-modules, where \(A\) and \(B\) carry the module structures induced by their structure maps.

A ring homomorphism \(\varphi \colon A \to B\) is an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism if and only if it is \(R\)-linear, meaning \(\varphi(r \cdot x) = r \cdot \varphi(x)\) for all \(r \in R\) and \(x \in A\).
blocks.proof:
Write \(r \cdot x := \alpha(r)x\) for the \(R\)-module structure on \(A\) and \(r \cdot y := \beta(r)y\) for that on \(B\). Suppose first that \(\varphi\) is an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism, so it is a ring homomorphism with \(\varphi \circ \alpha = \beta\). Then for all \(r \in R\) and \(x \in A\),
\[ \varphi(r \cdot x) = \varphi(\alpha(r)x) = \varphi(\alpha(r))\varphi(x) = \beta(r)\varphi(x) = r \cdot \varphi(x), \]
using multiplicativity of \(\varphi\) and the identity \(\varphi(\alpha(r)) = \beta(r)\). Since \(\varphi\) is additive it is therefore \(R\)-linear, and being also a ring homomorphism it is a morphism of \(R\)-modules and of rings. This establishes both equivalent characterizations from the definition. Conversely, suppose \(\varphi\) is a ring homomorphism that is \(R\)-linear. Applying \(R\)-linearity to \(x = 1_A\) and using \(\varphi(1_A) = 1_B\) gives
\[ \varphi(\alpha(r)) = \varphi(r \cdot 1_A) = r \cdot \varphi(1_A) = r \cdot 1_B = \beta(r)1_B = \beta(r), \]
so \(\varphi \circ \alpha = \beta\) and \(\varphi\) satisfies the defining compatibility. Hence the three formulations coincide.

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: For a fixed commutative ring \(R\), the \(R\)-algebras together with their \(R\)-algebra homomorphisms form a category: the identity map \(\mathrm{id}_A\) is an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism, and the composite of two \(R\)-algebra homomorphisms is again an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism.
blocks.proof:
Let \(A\) be an \(R\)-algebra with structure map \(\alpha \colon R \to A\). The identity \(\mathrm{id}_A \colon A \to A\) is a ring homomorphism, and \(\mathrm{id}_A \circ \alpha = \alpha\), so it satisfies the compatibility condition and is an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism. Now let \(\varphi \colon A \to B\) and \(\psi \colon B \to C\) be \(R\)-algebra homomorphisms, with structure maps \(\alpha \colon R \to A\), \(\beta \colon R \to B\), \(\gamma \colon R \to C\). The composite \(\psi \circ \varphi \colon A \to C\) is a ring homomorphism, being a composite of ring homomorphisms. Moreover
\[ (\psi \circ \varphi) \circ \alpha = \psi \circ (\varphi \circ \alpha) = \psi \circ \beta = \gamma, \]
using \(\varphi \circ \alpha = \beta\) and \(\psi \circ \beta = \gamma\). Thus \(\psi \circ \varphi\) commutes with the structure maps and is an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism. Associativity of composition and the unit laws are inherited from composition of functions, so the data assemble into a category.

blocks.label: Examples
items: Every ring is uniquely a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra, and every ring homomorphism is automatically a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra homomorphism, since any ring map necessarily respects the unique structure map \(\mathbb{Z} \to A\).

For the polynomial algebra \(R[x]\) and any \(R\)-algebra \(B\), choosing an element \(b \in B\) determines a unique \(R\)-algebra homomorphism \(R[x] \to B\) sending \(x \mapsto b\); this evaluation map is the universal property of \(R[x]\).

Over \(R = \mathbb{C}\), the identity \(\mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}\) is a \(\mathbb{C}\)-algebra homomorphism, but complex conjugation \(z \mapsto \bar{z}\), though a ring homomorphism, is not a \(\mathbb{C}\)-algebra homomorphism, as it fails \(\varphi(r \cdot 1) = r\) for non-real \(r\).

If \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq A\) is an ideal of an \(R\)-algebra \(A\), the canonical projection \(A \to A/\mathfrak{a}\) is an \(R\)-algebra homomorphism onto the quotient, which inherits its \(R\)-algebra structure via the composite \(R \to A \to A/\mathfrak{a}\).

concepts.inline: The polynomial algebra \(R[x]\) is the \(R\)-algebra of polynomials in one variable with coefficients in \(R\).

concepts.title: identity map
concepts.inline: The identity map on an object \(A\) is the morphism \(\mathrm{id}_A\) that sends every element to itself.

concepts.title: evaluation map
concepts.inline: The evaluation map is the \(R\)-algebra homomorphism \(R[x] \to B\) sending \(x\) to a chosen element \(b \in B\).

concepts.title: complex conjugation
concepts.inline: Complex conjugation is the ring automorphism of \(\mathbb{C}\) sending \(z = a+bi\) to \(\bar{z} = a-bi\).
